analysis.one_liner: Restricts smart devices and apps from collecting camera or microphone data without express consent.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop makers of internet-connected devices and apps from collecting camera or microphone data unless the collection is necessary for the device to function and happens only while the person is actively using it — or unless the person first gives express, affirmative consent. Voice-activated features could not listen before being switched on without separate consent. People could revoke consent from the device, the Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and companies could get advance FTC approval of their notices as a safe harbor.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, everyone who owns an internet-connected device — phones, laptops, smart speakers, TVs — would gain a legal guarantee that a camera or microphone is not collecting data behind their back, and a way to see and revoke any consent they gave. The FTC would have a clear mandate to police violations.

how_it_helps.text: Bars collecting, transmitting, or processing camera or microphone data unless it is needed for the device to work and collected only while the person is actively using it, unless the person gives express consent.
Requires separate, plain-language consent before voice-activated features like smart speakers ever start listening, and lets people revoke that consent from the device itself.
Makes violations enforceable by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice, and gives companies a safe harbor if the FTC approves their notices in advance.

analysis.who_pays: Device manufacturers and app developers would bear the cost of compliance: separate consent flows, plain-language notices, publicly posted privacy policies, and FTC enforcement exposure.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on device and app makers, which could slow or add expense to product development — a burden the bill's opponents would raise, though it does not fall on consumers directly.

The bill would not stop all data collection — uses consistent with reasonable consumer expectations and covered by affirmative consent remain legal, so camera and microphone data collection continues with notice rather than ending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to privacy and consumer control is real and the burden on companies modest: they already have screens and consent flows, and the FTC safe harbor rewards compliance. The main cost is FTC oversight and possible delays in shipping new voice features, plus the risk that consent prompts add friction. On balance the public benefit outweighs the industry cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs (R-NY) introduced the bill on October 22, 2021, with cosponsors Reps. Ed Case (D-HI) and John Rutherford (R-FL).
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on October 22, 2021, and to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce three days later.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting camera and microphone data never faced the restrictions, which never became law.

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Ed Case and John Rutherford

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a markup or reported the bill out before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor, one Republican cosponsor, and one Democratic cosponsor, so support was bipartisan but too small to generate any committee action.

industries.note: Would have to obtain separate affirmative consent before using camera or microphone data, restrict collection to active use, and publish plain-language privacy policies. Well-known brands already follow similar consent practices, so the burden is real but modest.

industries.industry: App developers, including voice-assistant and advertising-driven apps
industries.note: Loses the ability to quietly harvest audio or camera data when the app is not in use, limiting a source of ad-targeting data. Honest developers gain clearer FTC-approved rules of the road.
Gains a legal right to know when a device listens or watches and to say no or withdraw consent at any time.
